claims.text: Thermally activated atomic diffusion causes localized chemical segregation in the non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
Thermal evolution nucleates and grows Mg-rich intermetallic compounds, especially at grain and phase boundaries.
The newly formed Mg-rich phases mediate subsequent corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Mg-rich phases can promote a more adherent and protective oxide scale.
Mg-rich phases can alter local oxidation kinetics relative to the initial single-phase state.
The initial alloy is rapidly solidified, metastable, and single phase.
The initial alloy has a nominal density below 6 g/cm³.
The initial alloy contains Mg together with lightweight elements such as Al, Cu, Zn, and Gd.
Non-equilibrium rapid solidification suppresses equilibrium intermetallic formation in the initial alloy.
Controlled thermal aging or environmental exposure can initiate microstructural evolution in the alloy.
Aging temperatures sufficient to activate diffusion, while remaining below melting, enable diffusion-mediated phase segregation.
Discrete Mg-rich intermetallic phases form at grain boundaries and other microstructural heterogeneities.
Large constituent-property differences and the non-equilibrium processing history cause Mg to diffuse faster than the other elements.
Preferential Mg diffusion causes local chemical ordering and phase separation that produce Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The Mg-rich intermetallic phases can provide nucleation sites for a protective, self-healing oxide film.
The Mg-rich intermetallic phases can create local galvanic couples that accelerate or retard corrosion and oxidation.
Aged samples will contain measurable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the initial state.
Aging will change oxide-scale morphology or adhesion, corrosion-initiation sites, corrosion rates, and high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-cast baseline.
The proposed effect requires aging temperatures and exposure times sufficient for diffusion-mediated phase segregation and may disappear when diffusion is too slow.
